OBJECTIVES
The Shipping Corporation of India Limited works to fulfill its objective as mentioned below:
s To provide its clientele safe, environmentally sustainable, reliable, efficient and quality
 shipping services, complying with all legal and other requirements.
s To be an optimally profitable, viable, ethical and socially responsible commercial
 organization contributing to the national economy by securing a reasonable return on capital
 and serving the nation’s needs.
s To minimize risks and environmental impacts for achieving Safety, Occupational Health and 
 Environmental Performance.s To be a major player in India’s offshore and other marine activities and to continue to explore
 opportunities for  diversification for steady growth of the Company.
s To continually improve its efficiency in process and technology, adopting various measures
 including E-governance and optimum use of Information Technology.s To enhance competency and professionalism among its fleet and shore personnel through
 effective and dynamic Human Resource Management.s To own or acquire an adequate, well designed and efficient fleet to cater to the demand of
 global maritime trade through options like leasing, demise charter, joint ventures and other
 innovative financial measures.

The world GDP during 2025 grew by 2.9% and in 2026

prices on an average are expected to increase by 
about 22% in 2026 with industrial metal prices

increasing commodity prices, global headline 
inﬂation is expected to increase to 4% this year 
thereafter moderating to 3.1% next year. Growth in 
global goods and services trade is projected to 
decelerate from 4.8% in 2025 to 2.9% in 2026. 
Thereafter, Global trade growth is then projected to 
ﬁrm to an average of 3.2% in 2027–28, broadly in line 
with global output, as the adverse effects of tariffs 
and policy uncertainty ease. Recent Free Trade 
Agreements concluded between India and UK 
(India-UK CETA), India and Oman (India-Oman 
CEPA), India New Zealand FTA and India EU FTA in FY 
2025-26, are expected to support India Centric 
trade in the coming years.
Amidst, this broad-based slow down, South Asia,
particularly India, remain a positive factor for the 
industry with expected growth rate above 6.5%.
The Global Oil market is expected to improve in 
second half of 2026 following stabilization of trafﬁc 
through the Strait of Hormuz and softening of freight 
rates from current elevated levels with overall 
tonnage demand to improve in 2027 supported by 
rebound in global reﬁnery runs and a likely increase 
in inventory restocking. On the supply side, the crude 
tanker ﬂeet is projected to expand 5.6% by 2027, 
driven by a strong pipeline of new vessel deliveries 
despite a likely increase in scrapping activity. The 
current order book stands at around 22.9% of the 
existing ﬂeet, ensuring elevated deliveries over the 
next two years. While robust charter earnings are 
expected to limit demolitions in 2026, a potential 
decline in demand for sanctioned and shadow-
ﬂeet tonnage could trigger a modest increase in 
scrapping. Demolitions are expected to accelerate 
from 2027 as declining freight rates, improving ﬂeet 
availability and tightening environmental and 
regulatory requirements place growing pressure on 
older vessels, particularly those operating within the 
shadow ﬂeet. Product tankers, on the other hand, with

With his extensive industry experience, strategic vision, and unwavering 
commitment to organisational excellence and employee development, Capt. Som 
Raj continues to play a pivotal role in advancing SCI's growth and strengthening its 
position as India's premier shipping company.Capt. Som Raj assumed charge as Director (Personnel & Administration) of The 
Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. (SCI) with effect from 15 July 2025. He  is also a 
Director on the Board of Inland & Coastal Shipping Ltd. (ICSL), a wholly owned 
subsidiary of SCI. Earlier, he held the additional charge of Director (Finance), SCI 
from 1st January 2026 to 22nd February 2026. He was also a Director (Operations),

the National Maritime Day Celebrations (Central) Committee.
Capt. Som Raj is a seasoned maritime professional with over 35 years of experience 
in ship operations, human resource management, and maritime training. He 
began his career with The Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. in 1990 as a Trainee 
Nautical Ofﬁcer and progressed through the ranks to become a Ship Master in 
2005.
Following his transition ashore in 2007, he held several key leadership positions, 
including Marine Superintendent, Group In-charge (Quality & Safety), Principal of 
SCI's Maritime Training Institute, and General Manager (Fleet Personnel). Prior to 
assuming the position of Director (Personnel & Administration), he served as 
General Manager In-charge (Personnel & Administration). In this role, he oversaw 
the welfare and administration of nearly 3,000 seafarers and shore employees, 
managed industrial relations, led wage negotiations and regulatory 
engagements, and supervised the administration and maintenance of SCI's shore 
establishments.
During his career, he has also been associated with several strategic national 
initiatives, including SCI's support for ISRO's Mars Orbiter Mission and ensuring 
operational readiness for the Hon'ble Prime Minister's visit to Shri Vijay Puram. As 
Chairman of the Organising Committee of the National Maritime Day Celebrations 
(Central) Committee, he provides leadership in the planning and coordination of 
one of India's premier maritime events.His leadership has contributed to reducing vessel off-hire periods, optimising 
manpower deployment, and strengthening operational coordination with key 
stakeholders, including the Geological Survey of India (GSI), Oil and Natural Gas 
Corporation (ONGC), and the Andaman & Nicobar Administration.

19.  Transfer of Unclaimed or Unpaid Dividend and/or 
Shares to IEPF:
I. Members are requested to note that, pursuant to 
Section 124 of the Companies Act 2013, dividends 
which remain unpaid or unclaimed for a period of 7 
years from the date of transfer to Unpaid Dividend 
Account of the Company, are liable to be transferred 
to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (“IEPF”). 
The Shares in respect of which dividend has not been 
paid or claimed for seven consecutive years are also 
liable to be transferred to the Demat account of the 
IEPF Authority. In view of this, Members are requested to 
claim their dividends from the Company/RTA, and 
submit the required documents for issue of 
Entitlement Letter within the stipulated timeline.
II. In the event of transfer of shares and the unclaimed 
dividends to IEPF, Members are entitled to claim the 
same from the IEPF authority by submitting an online 
application in the prescribed Form IEPF-5 available 
on the website http://www.iepf.gov.in/  and sending 
a physical copy of the same duly signed to the

thYour Directors have pleasure in presenting the 76 Annual Report on the working of your Company for the 
stFinancial Year ended 31 March, 2026.
State of Company’s affairs
The Tanker segment recorded revenue of `3,942.23 crore during FY 2025–26, compared to `3,609.60 crore in 
the previous ﬁnancial year. Segment proﬁt increased signiﬁcantly from ` 680.14 crore in FY 2024–25 to `1,189.54 
crore in FY 2025–26. While revenue registered a moderate growth, proﬁtability improved substantially due to 
favourable market conditions and a higher number of time charter days, resulting in increased earnings. At 
the same time, improved ﬂeet deployment and operational efﬁciencies helped optimise operating expenses, 
leading to a proportionately higher increase in segment proﬁt than in revenue. The Bulk segment recorded 
revenue of ` 788.87 crore in FY 2025–26 as against ` 711.29 crore in FY 2024–25. The segment's loss reduced from 
`22.24 crore to ` 19.11 crore during the year. The increase in revenue was primarily driven by a higher number of 
voyage charters and a marginal improvement in market conditions. However, the gains were partially offset 
by higher operating expenses, resulting in only a modest reduction in the segment's loss. Revenue from the 
Liner segment declined to `784.27 crore in FY 2025–26 from `1,036.23 crore in FY 2024–25. The segment reported 
a proﬁt of `74.84 crore, compared to `166.22 crore in the previous year. The decline in both revenue and 
proﬁtability was primarily attributable to lower freight rates and reduced cargo volumes during the year. The 
T&OS segment recorded revenue of ` 297.85 crore in FY 2025–26, compared to ` 276.19 crore in FY 2024–25. 
Segment proﬁt increased marginally from `32.48 crore to ` 35.29 crore. Although revenue improved during the 
year, the increase in proﬁtability remained modest due to higher operating expenses.

SPECIAL PURPOSE VEHICLE:incorporated on 29.09.2016 to promote inland waterways transport.
Work was suspended on September 17, 2007, due to an interim stay order from Hon’ble Supreme Court, 
regarding dredging operations in the Adam's Bridge area. All dredgers were subsequently withdrawn by July 
27, 2009, as a final decision on an alternative alignment remained pending. A Supreme Court hearing 
scheduled for April 6, 2018, was indefinitely withheld.B. SCI Bharat IFSC Limited
SCI Bharat IFSC Ltd. is a wholly-owned subsidiary of The Shipping Corporation of India Limited. As the Company 
is currently in its formative stage, its business activities during the financial year 2025–26 remained limited 
and exploring to increase business in various fields. However, with the growing opportunities available within 
the International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) ecosystem, the Company expects its business operations to 
expand significantly in the coming years. 
The Government of India established Sethusamudram Corporation Limited (SCL) to fund and manage the 
Sethusamudram Ship Channel Project, aiming to create a navigable channel from the Gulf of Mannar to the 
Bay of Bengal through Palk Bay. As mandated by the government, various PSUs, including SCI, were to 
contribute equity to this project. By FY 2016-17, SCI had invested ₹50 crore.
At its meeting held on August 9, 2024, the Board of Directors of SCI approved the nomination of Rear Admiral 
Jaswinder Singh, (Retd.) Director (L&PS) as SCI’s representative on the Board of Sethusamudram Corporation 
Ltd (SCL), subject to the approval of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW). Following MoPSW's 
advice that the earlier established procedure be followed, as per which, SCI may directly appoint a Nominee 
Director to the SCL Board. Accordingly, at its meeting held on November 8, 2024, the SCI Board granted 
approval for the appointment of the Director (L&PS) as a Nominee Director on the SCL Board to represent SCI. As on 31.03.2026, ICSL is managing & operating 6 IWAI owned vessels comprising cargo vessels, RORO vessels & 
passenger catamaran.ICSL has been designated as the implementing agency for establishing scheduled cargo services on National 
Waterways-1 and National Waterways-2, i.e., Haldia/Kolkata to Varanasi (NW-1) and Kolkata to Dhubri/Pandu (NW-2), 
under the Jal Vahak Scheme, a promotional initiative announced by the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways 
(MoPSW) in December 2024 to enhance cargo movement through Inland Waterways Transport (IWT).
To support this growth, the Company has initiated a series of strategic and transformative measures aimed 
at establishing a sustainable and robust business model. In this regards, the Company is in the process of 
appointing a reputed business consultant with global expertise in financial services and business 
development. Simultaneously, concerted efforts are being undertaken at both the Company and Ministry 
levels to formulate comprehensive governance frameworks, strengthen organisational structures, 
streamline operational processes and establish systems and controls that are aligned with international best 
practices. These initiatives are intended to create a sustainable growth, enhancing stakeholder confidence 
and supporting the Company's long-term business expansion. 
The Board of Sethusamudram Corporation Ltd. thereafter appointed Director (L&PS) as an Additional Director 
of SCL on February 4, 2025.

The Non-Executive Part-Time Ex-Officio Directors (Government Directors) do not draw any 
remuneration/sitting fees from the Company for their roles as Director but draw their remuneration under 
Central Dearness Allowance (CDA) scale  from the Government as government official.Being a Government Company within the meaning of Section 2(45) of the Companies Act, 2013, the prior 
approval of the President of India is required for appointment to the posts of Board-level Directors. 
Accordingly, the authority for appointment of Directors to the Board of the Company rests with the 
Government of India, and the terms and conditions governing the appointment of Directors are determined 
by the Government of India.
SCI considers Risk Management to be a core component of the Management of the Company and its ability to 
identify and address risks is central to achieving Corporate objectives. Accordingly, SCI has developed a 
detailed Risk Management Policy in line with the requirements of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, which includes 
framework for identification of risks, measures for risk mitigation and Business Continuity Plan. The Policy has 
been approved by the Risk Management Committee and the Board. 
I) Strategic Risk  ii) Operational Risk  iii) Financial Risk  iv) Compliance Risk
Some of the risks identified by SCI include market volatility, increasing bunkering cost, cyber security risk, geo-
political risks, decarbonisation challenges, Piracy, Foreign exchange fluctuation, regulatory compliances 
among others. All efforts are made for mitigating and controlling the risks through well-defined mitigation 
measures and coordination with all stakeholders.
SCI has formulated a three line of Risk Reporting viz. Corporate Risk Committee, Risk Management Committee

A Special Crisis Management Team (CMT) has been formed to monitor and assist vessels trading in War Zone 
Areas of West Asia Gulf Region and Strait of Hormuz.  The Team is monitoring vessels closely on 24x7 basis. 
Considering heightened Safety/Security concerns and volatile situations prevailing across the West Asia Gulf 
Region / Persian Gulf / HRA areas, SCI HO Crisis Management Control Room / Contingency Room is being 
maintained & monitored daily on a 24x7 basis to provide immediate support and necessary help to our fleet 
vessels trading in above region. Additional war risk premium is taken on case to case basis for vessels 
transiting the above high risk areas.The Risk Management Policy is uploaded on the website of the Company at the following link:

iii] STRENGTHS
SCI remains India's largest and most diversified shipping company, backed by over six decades of operational 
experience across multiple shipping segments. The Company operates a balanced fleet comprising crude oil 
tankers, product tankers, LPG carriers, bulk carriers, container vessels, offshore support vessels, and LNG 
carriers through its joint ventures. This diversified fleet profile helps mitigate cyclicality in individual shipping 
sectors while enabling SCI to capitalize on opportunities across different maritime markets.
B).  BULK CARRIERS & TANKERS
1)  Crude Oil & Product Tankers
The tanker market during financial year 2025-26 witnessed a strong recovery in earnings and tonnage 
utilization, driven primarily by geopolitical disruptions, changing crude oil trade patterns, tightening effective 
vessel supply and increasing tonne-mile demand. The market remained highly volatile but overall favorable 
for tankers particularly in the crude oil segment. The crude tanker market experienced one of its strongest 
phases since the post-covid recovery, particularly from third quarter of financial year 2025-26 onwards. 
Although earnings moderated in the first half of 2025, market conditions strengthened in later part of 2025 as 
OPEC+ accelerated its production unwinding plans and China increased crude oil stockpiling. Fleet growth 
remained constrained as an expanding sanctioned fleet and a limited number of new deliveries restricted 
effective supply, providing sustained support to freight rates. The acquisition of two modern gas carriers further strengthens SCI's presence in the gas transportation 
segment, enhances its fleet profile, and positions the Company to capitalize on the growing demand for LPG 
and gas transportation driven by India's expanding energy requirements.
At the same time, product tanker owners experienced a mixed market in 2025, as increase in newbuilding 
deliveries brought earnings under pressure. Although freight rates remained subdued in the first half of 2025, 
conditions improved in the second half of 2025, supported by the strong crude tanker market. However, crude 
tanker market was quite buoyant and a number of LR2 product tankers switched to dirty trades owing to 
elevated Aframax earnings. This effectively tightened supply in the clean segment. Meanwhile, Europe’s plans 
to ban refined products derived from Russian crude benefited MR tankers as the transatlantic diesel flows 
from the US to Europe increased ahead of the winter season.
Global Oil demand in the year 2025 was marginally higher compared to the demand during year 2024. The 
market was primarily driven by various factors including India reducing dependence on Russian crude, 
increased long-haul imports from the US Gulf as well as the geo-political disruptions in the Middle East Gulf, 
Venezuela and the Red Sea region, which resulted in growing Asian stockpiling activity. The easing of US 
sanctions on Venezuela boosted Venezuelan exports, increasing employment of mainstream vessels. These 
factors boosted trading activity and underpinned the demand for tankers. VLCC freight rates surged to 
exceptionally high levels in September 2025, driven by heightened demand against the backdrop of minimal 
fleet additions.The Company's fleet is strategically deployed across India's EXIM trade, coastal trade, and international cross-
trade routes, providing flexibility in vessel employment and revenue generation. SCI continues to enjoy a 
unique position in the Indian maritime sector as the only Indian shipping company operating both coastal 
and international container liner services. Additionally, through its joint venture companies, SCI maintains a 
presence in the LNG transportation sector, a strategically important segment supporting India's growing 
energy requirements.

On the tonnage supply side, first quarter of 2026 saw deliveries of 27 crude tankers (5.5 mdwt), which is

additions. The current tanker new building order book represents about 23% of the fleet. Based on the current 
orderbook position, a further 66 tankers (13.9 mdwt) are scheduled for delivery in the remainder of 2026 with 
Suezmax and VLCC vessels dominating the new additions. For Product tankers, as per reports, around 70 non-

is also important to note that more than 200 tankers are currently stuck in the Middle East Gulf and there 
rejoining the active fleet is also important for the supply situation.In the recent years, the crude tanker sector has been impacted by geopolitical and trade related 
developments resulting in significant volatility in freight markets. With the disruption to crude oil exports from 
Middle East Gulf owing to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, the crude tanker market has entered yet 
another turbulent phase as around 10 mbpd of crude oil has been effectively trapped within the Middle East 
Gulf. Prior to the West Asia conflict, global oil demand was projected to grow by around 0.8 mbpd in 2026 
compared with 2025, supported by lower crude prices resulting from the unwinding of OPEC+ production cuts 
and a recovery in petrochemical feedstock demand. However, the ongoing disruption to Middle Eastern 
supply and the resultant high oil prices have significantly altered the outlook. Global oil demand is now 
expected to contract in 2026 amid tight supply and elevated prices; however, With significant inventory 
drawdowns due to disrupted crude flows and precautionary stock releases, the reopening of SOH, refiners 
and governments will replenish the depleted inventories, supporting crude trade and tanker demand during 
second half 2026 and into 2027.
Looking ahead beyond the current MEG conflict scenario, overall tonnage demand is expected to improve, 
supported by a rebound in global refinery runs and a likely increase in inventory restocking as rebuilding of oil 
stocks shall support post-war tanker demand growth. Any sustained oversupply in the global oil market 
stemming from the unwinding of OPEC+ production cuts could provide additional support to crude trade 
volumes, tonnage demand, and tanker earnings. Any reconfiguration of trade patterns will be an opportunity 
for the VLCC tonnage and will boost tonne-mile demand. Further Asia-bound trade is likely to surge due to 
such restocking activity. It will provide firm support to freight rates. The partial relaxation of sanctions of The average spot rate yield (TCE) of TD3C route (AG/China for VLCC) was US$ 80,000 per day in 2025. In case of

Although, the immediate shocks were felt in energy shipping, multiple sectors have been exposed, with knock-

2)  Dry Bulk
The overall dry bulk segment earnings for the year FY 25-26 was healthier as compared to FY 24-25. The 
average Baltic Dry Index (BDI) firmed up slightly in FY 25-26 when compared to FY 24-25 and the TCY earning 
stalso improved. Although the market for Dry Bulk Carriers was subdued in 1 half of 2025-26, the markets 
improved substantially in the second half. The key differentiator was Jan – March 2026 period where in, the BDI Venezuelan crude is expected to move on compliant mainstream tonnage. The Aframax demand is likely to 
be strengthened, as these vessels dominate the short-haul routes from Venezuela to the US. While global 
refined product trade is projected to rebound on the back of stronger refinery activity and increased 
inventory replenishment, growth in vessel supply is likely to outpace demand growth. After contracting in 2026 
due to the disruption to the refined product flows caused by SOH blockade, the global clean petroleum 
product (CPP) trade is projected to expand once the blockade is lifted. Higher refinery runs, improved crude 
availability and a gradual normalisation of trade flows are likely to support this recovery.
Since the beginning of the West Asia conflict, the Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed and as of now it 
remains unknown when the strait will reopen. The reduction in global crude oil supply has led to increase in the 
price of crude, which has led many countries to take emergency steps to deal with the energy crisis. The higher 
oil prices have already impacted global inflation levels. In order to keep inflation in check, central banks may 
be forced to raise interest rates, which may slow economic activity.
After the SOH blockade, buyers secured alternative barrels from Atlantic Basin suppliers such as West Africa, 
Latin America, and the US. This shift significantly boosted tonnage demand in Atlantic loading regions. 
Although freight rates have since eased from their immediate post-conflict levels as vessel repositioning 
improved tonnage availability at loading hubs, they remain well above 2025 averages. Nevertheless, if the 
blockade continues, subdued crude trade volumes will increasingly weigh on vessel employment, eventually 
exerting downward pressure on freight rates. The future trajectory of tanker earnings will therefore depend 
heavily on the duration of the disruption. The longer the blockade persists, the greater the damage to tonnage 
demand and vessel earnings.
In case of product tankers, restrictions on clean product exports continue to limit export opportunities in Asia. 
Although intra-Asia trade initially benefited from reduced Middle Eastern supply, sustained declines in refinery 
runs amid tight crude availability are likely to erode these gains and weaken regional tanker demand. A similar 
trend is seen to be emerging in Europe. Any further slowdown in refinery activity is likely to reduce intra-
European diesel movements and transatlantic gasoline trade, which will affect product tanker demand. A 
potential resolution of the Russia-Ukraine conflict could lead to resumption of short-haul Russian diesel. 
However, the weakness in refined products trade resulting from the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz is now 
being reflected in the freight rates. The future direction of the product tanker market is largely dependent on 
the duration of the disruption. If the blockade persists for an extended period, it will hamper global refined 
product trade, undermining tonne-mile demand and putting downward pressure on freight rates.The global oil market will remain extremely tight due to the disruption to MEG exports. Even likely expansion in 
non-OPEC supply – particularly with rising crude production from Latin America and parts of the Atlantic Basin 
– will not be sufficient to fully offset the loss of MEG supply. This might lead to under supply in the market making 
it highly vulnerable to further price spikes in the near term. It may be noted that the International Energy 
Agency (IEA), in its latest forecast, has lowered its estimates of global oil supply as well as that for refinery 
throughput and demand for 2026 compared to the pre-war forecasts. Any prolonged extension of the 
blockade is likely to dent tonnage demand and place significant downward pressure on freight rates.

Risks & Concerns
The US/Israel–Iran conflict and closure of Strait of Hormuz has adversely impacted movement of Fertilizer and 
also has led to loss of access to the Persian Gulf markets. Although the war has led to the markets temporarily 
firming up, any prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz may lead to changes in global trade flow and 
dependence of non renewal energy, which was dampen the demand in long term.
The global Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) market is entering a period of significant expansion driven by rising 
energy demand, increasing export capacity, and long-term energy security strategies across major 
importing nations. Global LNG trade reached approximately 435 million tonnes in 2025 as compared to 412 
million tonnes in 2024 and is expected to continue growing strongly through 2030. New liquefaction projects in 
the United States, Qatar, and Canada are expected to add nearly 290 million tonnes per annum (mtpa) of 
export capacity by the end of the decade.
Geopolitical developments remain a key market risk. The disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz 
during Q1 of 2026 demonstrated the vulnerability of global LNG supply chains and caused extreme volatility in 
LNG freight markets. Spot LNG carrier rates surged above $200,000 per day during the peak of the crisis before 
moderating. Overall, the global LNG industry is positioned for sustained growth through 2030. While short-term 
market volatility and fleet oversupply may create challenges, the long-term outlook remains positive, 
supported by expanding production capacity, growing international trade, and increasing demand for 
cleaner energy sources worldwide. Geopolitical and weather-related factors will remain key swing factors, 
along with China’s demand recovery. US-led policy changes may also dictate the market shifts.China remains central to the dry bulk market due to its dominance in iron ore, coal, and steel-related trades. 
Weaker demand from key commodities, particularly coal and iron ore, driven by a slowdown in China, would 
weigh on cargo volumes.
Also, a sudden de-escalation and opening of Strait of Hormuz may also lead to oversupply of tonnage in 
certain areas, which may lead to a fall in the market. 
Lastly, the Middle East war has had impact on bunker prices and thus volatility of bunker prices remains a point 
of concern.

The United States is expected to remain the world's largest LNG exporter, supported by the ramp-up of major 
projects such as Plaquemines’ LNG and Corpus Christi Stage 3. Qatar's North Field expansion and LNG 
Canada's continued development will further contribute to supply growth. Demand growth is expected to be 
led by Europe and Asia. European imports remain supported by energy security requirements, while Asian 
demand is forecast to strengthen as economic growth and cleaner energy policies drive gas consumption.3) LNG and LPG scenario:
LNG shipping demand is projected to increase alongside trade growth. The market is expected to shift from a

is projected to rise 6.4% YoY to approximately 458 million tonnes in 2026. Looking ahead, continued investment 
in LNG infrastructure, long-term supply agreements, and rising global energy demand support a positive 
long-term outlook for the sector. 
Global LPG trade is expected to grow at 3.6% CAGR (2025–2030), slower than the 4.3% CAGR seen in 2020–2024. 
Asia will remain the largest demand centre, led by India, Indonesia, and emerging Southeast Asian markets.  
Petrochemical demand, especially from China, will be the key driver and uncertainty for future LPG imports.

India’s LNG ScenarioUS–China trade diversification is reshaping LPG flows, leading to longer shipping routes and higher ton-mile 
demand.  LPG shipping in 2026 will be driven by geopolitical disruptions, particularly reduced Middle Eastern 
exports through the Strait of Hormuz. Middle Eastern LPG supply is expected to fall sharply, while increased US 
exports can only partially offset the shortage, keeping the market tight. Freight rates have risen due to limited 
vessel availability and longer trade routes, but high LPG prices are weakening downstream demand. Although 
near-term market conditions remain supportive, rapid fleet growth in 2026–27 could create vessel oversupply 
and pressure freight rates over the medium term.
India's LNG imports declined to just under 25 million tonnes, a 9% year-on-year decrease.  Main reasons 
included subdued power-sector and industrial gas demand, high competition from coal, buyers delaying 
purchases in anticipation of increased global LNG supply in 2026 and elevated LNG prices, which encouraged 
consumers to switch from PNG (piped natural gas) to propane. 
India currently has 8 LNG terminals and combined regasification capacity of 52.7 mtpa.  However only the 
terminal at Dahej LNG Terminal operated above 90% utilisation in 2025. Most other terminals are running below 
30% utilisation. This is expected to improve with the completion of the breakwater at Chhara LNG Terminal, 
Expansion of Dahej LNG Terminal by 5 mtpa and proposed Gopalpur LNG Terminal project. Important projects 
also include MNJPL and URJA South Link
India’s Domestic Gas Production Remains Limited. Domestic production supplied approximately 50% of India's 
gas demand in FY 2023-24. But production growth is expected to be modest: Only about 8% higher by 2030 
compared with 2023 levels. Reasons include maturing gas fields, production variability and allocation policy 
constraints. As a result India's LNG imports will likely need to double by 2030 if the country aims to increase 
natural gas's share in the energy mix to 15%. 
India signed nearly 10 mtpa of LNG supply agreements with Qatar, United Arab Emirates, and United States. 
Benefits would include reduced dependence on a single supplier and greater contractual flexibility.
Your company jointly owns and operates 3 LNG carriers under long term charters with charterers Petronet LNG 
Limited, India for transportation of LNG predominantly from Qatar. The 4th LNG carrier is under long term 
charter to Exxon Mobil LNG Services B.V, Netherlands. In order to ensure its presence in the new areas of the LNG 
market, your company is exploring new opportunities in LNG space through exploring collaborative strategic 
partnerships. Your company has built up a pool of trained LNG officers and the experience of independent 
technical operation of LNG tankers has helped to provide ship management services. The government plans to mandate LNG terminals to maintain additional storage equal to 10% of terminal 
capacity that can be accessed during supply disruptions or price shocks. This would effectively create India's 
strategic natural gas reserve.
India has around 25,000 km of operational gas pipelines and another 9,000 km under construction, yet 
pipeline utilisation is only about 40%.These pipelines are intended to support CGD networks, CNG stations, 
industrial consumers and residential gas users. 
India's LNG imports were expected to rise from 24 million tonnes in 2025 to 26 million tonnes in 2026 due to 
growing industrial demand and expansion of natural gas use. However, conflict-related disruptions have 
weakened this outlook because India depends heavily on Middle Eastern suppliers, particularly Qatar and 
United Arab Emirates, which together account for about half of India's LNG imports. During the first quarter of 
2026, LNG imports fell to 5.2 million tonnes, a 7% year-on-year decline. Despite disruptions, India mitigated 
some supply losses by sourcing LNG from the United States and Nigeria.

India’s LPG Scenario
Around 90% of India's LPG imports come from the Middle East. Imports fell sharply from about 1.9 million tonnes 
in January–February to 0.9 million tonnes in March after the disruption. Total LPG imports declined 26% 
quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) and 12% year-on-year (YoY) in Q1 2026. India is particularly vulnerable because 
residential LPG demand is structurally strong and relatively inelastic, domestic production covers only a 
portion of demand and import dependence remains high despite efforts to diversify supply sources. 
The Indian government has taken remedial measures such as refineries and petrochemical companies were 
instructed to maximize LPG production, Propane, butane, propylene, and butane streams were redirected into 
LPG production, domestic LPG output reportedly increased by 25% and additional supply was allocated 
primarily to households. Priority access was extended to essential sectors such as hospitals and educational 
institutions. A committee consisting of executives from oil majors was established to manage allocations to 
commercial users such as restaurants and hotels. India sought alternative suppliers such as Argentina which 
increased LPG exports to India to 50,000 tonnes in Q1 2026, more than double 2025 levels. Existing supply 
agreements with Chevron, Phillips 66 and Total Energies provided 2.2 million tonnes of US LPG during 2026, 
helping offset some Middle East shortages.

7.0 Industry Structure and Developments: 
i) World scenario:
 The Offshore Support Vessel (OSV) industry is closely linked to offshore exploration and production (E&P)
 activities, rig utilization levels and overall investments in offshore oil and gas fields. The sector is
 significantly influenced by global energy security strategies, Government policies, long-term crude oil
 price trends and capital expenditure plans of major oil and gas companies.
 Despite such challenges, the global OSV market has witnessed gradual improvement in utilization levels
 and charter rates, particularly for modern and technologically advanced offshore assets. The market
 dynamics in several regions have shifted from a charterers’ market towards a relatively balanced or
 owners’ market, especially for high-specification vessels. Further, increasing investments in offshore
 renewable energy projects are also expected to support long-term demand for specialized offshore
 support vessels. Global economic uncertainties, geopolitical tensions, recessionary pressures in developed economies,
 the Russia–Ukraine conflict, tensions in the Middle East, evolving global trade dynamics and tariff-related
 developments continue to influence the outlook of the offshore sector and may impact future investment
 decisions in offshore exploration and production activities.

 Reserves and Exploration: India possesses significant offshore hydrocarbon reserves, particularly in the
 western offshore region of the Arabian Sea and the eastern offshore region of the Bay of Bengal.
 Exploration activities continue in both shallow-water and deep-water blocks, including identification of
 new reserves in deep-water and ultra-deep-water areas. Recent tenders floated by ONGC have witnessed intense competition from both Indian private operators
 and foreign vessel owners. Such competitive pressure has moderated the extent of increase in charter
 hire rates in the Indian market as compared to certain international offshore markets, although charter
 rates have shown improvement over the subdued levels witnessed in previous years.
 Technological Advancements: Continuous advancements in seismic imaging, drilling technologies,
 digital monitoring systems and enhanced oil recovery techniques are improving operational efficiency
 and enabling commercially viable offshore operations in deeper and technically challenging
 environments. The outlook for the Indian offshore oil and gas industry continues to remain positive, supported by
 increasing energy demand, continued exploration activities, Government policy initiatives and
 technological advancements in offshore operations. The Indian OSV market is primarily driven by offshore activities of state-owned oil and gas companies,
 predominantly ONGC, with substantial operations across the Western Offshore region, including Mumbai
 High and Bassein fields, as well as the Eastern Offshore region in the Krishna-Godavari Basin.

D. PERSONNEL AND ADMINISTRATION
In response to these industry challenges, the Fleet Personnel Department of The Shipping Corporation of India 
Ltd. (SCI) has adopted a multi-pronged strategy focussed on strengthening both recruitment and retention of 
seafarers. Key initiatives undertaken during the year included market-aligned wage enhancements, career 
progression opportunities through parallel sailing arrangements for senior officers, regularisation of eligible 
officers, rejoining incentives, family carriage facilities, and focussed recruitment drives. These initiatives have 
resulted in improved manning levels, particularly for offshore vessels and Special Trade Passenger Ships.
The Collective Bargaining Agreements (CBAs), namely the National Maritime Board (NMB) Agreement 
applicable to Ratings and Petty Officers and the INSA-MUI Agreement applicable to Officers, continue to 
remain in force and are valid up to 31 December 2027.
As on 31 March 2026, SCI had an onboard strength of 2,267 seafarers. The Company's workforce comprised 
1000 Regular Personnel, while 1,267 personnel were engaged on direct contract. SCI continues to maintain an 
adequate and competent manpower pool to meet its present operational requirements and support future 
business growth.The global maritime industry continues to face a significant shortage of qualified seafarer officers. Reports 
published by the Baltic and International Maritime Council (BIMCO) and the International Chamber of 
Shipping (ICS) have highlighted the widening gap between the demand for and supply of competent officers, 
driven by the continued expansion of the global merchant fleet. This shortage is evident across all ranks and 
vessel segments, including Bulk Carriers, Special Trade Passenger Ships, offshore vessels, and vessels 
requiring Near Coastal Voyage (NCV) certified officers.
The Company also maintains a robust pipeline of future officers by inducting Deck Cadets, Engine Cadets, and 
Trainee Electrical Officers into the regular roster upon successful completion of shipboard training and 
acquisition of Certificates of Competency (CoC), in accordance with the provisions of the INSA-MUI 
Agreement. Further more, 2nd Mates and Marine Engineer Officers (MEO) Class IV officers are inducted from 
the open market to bridge identified  gaps and ensure continuity in officer availability.A. FLEET PERSONNEL
SCI continues to strengthen its talent acquisition efforts by regularly advertising vacancies on the Company's 
website and expanding its outreach through social media platforms to attract qualified maritime 
professionals. Officers are recruited both directly and through approved manning agencies to ensure timely 
availability of competent personnel for operational requirements.

The Company has a Board-approved accounting policy dated 17.05.2024 for recognition of interest on 
Income Tax refunds, under which interest income is recognised upon receipt of the refund amount. The 
accounting treatment adopted during the financial year 2025–26 is in accordance with this policy, which has 
been consistently followed over the years, considering the practical uncertainties associated with the receipt 
of Income Tax refunds and the related interest.The observation relates to the disclosures prescribed under Ind AS 20. While the financial statements did not 
specifically include a) the accounting policy on Government grants, including the method of presentation in 
the financial statements, and b) an explicit disclosure regarding unfulfilled conditions and other 
contingencies attached to the recognised Government assistance, the Company confirms that no such 
unfulfilled conditions or contingencies existed in respect of the grant recognised during the financial year 
2025–26.
The observation is disclosure-related in nature and does not affect the recognition, measurement or 
presentation of the grant, or the profit for the year, total comprehensive income, cash flows or net worth of the 
Company.
The Company has taken note of the observation and will strengthen the accounting policy and related 
disclosures on Government grants in future financial statements to ensure full compliance with the 
disclosure requirements of Ind AS 20.
Management Response on Comment No. 2
The Company has taken note of the observation of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India and will 
review the existing accounting policy and related disclosures in light of the observation and the applicable 
requirements of the Indian Accounting Standards. Appropriate modifications, wherever considered 
necessary, will be incorporated in future financial statements.

 4. CSR Initiatives:  Our community engagement initiatives positively impacted the lives of multiple
individuals and many families, focussing on education, healthcare and livelihood opportunities across 
diverse communities. 2. Waste Management:  Waste generated on board during normal operation of the ship is managed as
  per the vessel-specific garbage management plan and landed ashore at approved reception
  facilities for further processing. Also, the discharge of oil, solid waste & sewage etc. from its ships is
  prohibited under MARPOL (International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships). Most of
  our vessels comply with Green Passport or equivalent notation. In addition, the Company diligently
  adheres to the compliance requirements specified in the administration circular concerning the
  Transport and Handling of hazardous and noxious liquid substances in bulk on Indian-flagged
  offshore support vessels.ESG Related Challenges: Over the past year, we have encountered a range of ESG challenges that have

outside our organisation continues to be a priority for us.

Category Process adopted for safe reclaiming / reuse / recycling / disposal
(a) Plastics 
(including 
packaging)Plastic waste generated onboard vessels is managed in accordance with the Ship-specific 
Garbage Management Plan and the requirements of MARPOL Annex V. Plastic waste is 
segregated at source and retained onboard until it is delivered to authorised Port Reception 
Facilities (PRFs) for environmentally sound disposal or recycling. The Company has also 
eliminated the use of Single Use Plastics (SUP) onboard its vessels in compliance with the 
Directorate General of Shipping guidelines. Wherever operationally feasible, suppliers are 
encouraged to minimise packaging waste and use recyclable or environmentally friendly 
packaging materials.
(b) E-waste Electronic and electrical waste generated at shore establishments is collected separately and 
disposed of through authorised e-waste recyclers in accordance with the applicable 
provisions of the E-Waste (Management) Rules. Obsolete electronic equipment generated 
onboard vessels is disposed of through authorised facilities or approved recyclers during port 
calls or dry docking, wherever applicable.
(c) 
Hazardous 
WasteHazardous waste including waste oil, oily sludge, oil filters, contaminated rags, chemical 
containers, paint residues, batteries, fluorescent lamps, pyrotechnics and other hazardous 
materials generated during vessel operations are handled, stored and disposed of in 
accordance with MARPOL, applicable environmental regulations and Shipboard Oil Pollution 
Emergency Plans (SOPEP), wherever applicable. Such waste is handed over only to authorised Port 
Reception Facilities or authorised recyclers for environmentally sound treatment and disposal.
(d) Other 
WasteFood waste, domestic waste, sewage and operational waste generated onboard vessels are 
managed in accordance with MARPOL requirements, Garbage Management Plans and 
Sewage Management Systems. Scrap generated during vessel repairs and dry docking is 
handed over to authorised shipyards or recyclers for recycling. The Company also complies 
with the Hong Kong International Convention for the Safe and Environmentally Sound Recycling 
of Ships, 2009 through maintenance of the Inventory of Hazardous Materials (IHM) and adoption 
of environmentally sound ship recycling practices.ANNEXURE II - BUSINESS RESPONSIBILITY & SUSTAINABILITY REPORT

3. Describe the processes in place to safely reclaim your products for reusing, recycling and disposing at the 
end of life, for (a) Plastics (including packaging) (b) E-waste (c) Hazardous waste and (d) other waste.
Reply: 
The Company is engaged in the business of shipping and marine transportation and does not manufacture 
products requiring end-of-life reclamation. However, it has established procedures for the safe management 
and disposal of operational waste generated on board vessels and at shore establishments in accordance 
with applicable national regulations and the International Maritime Organization (IMO) MARPOL Convention.
Garbage, including plastics, is segregated, stored and disposed of through approved port reception facilities 
in compliance with MARPOL Annex V. Food waste is managed using approved food waste comminutors and 
food waste freezers, as applicable. Sewage is treated through approved Sewage Treatment Plants and 
discharged in accordance with MARPOL Annex IV. Oily water and other technical waste are managed using 
approved 15 ppm Oily Water Separators, Oil Discharge Monitoring Systems and other pollution prevention 
equipment in compliance with MARPOL Annex I. E-waste generated on board and at shore establishments is 
disposed of through authorized recyclers or approved waste management agencies in accordance with 
applicable statutory requirements.

To reduce emissions, the Company has implemented/ taken following initiatives:
(ii) Reducing SOx emissions from its ships to improve air quality & reduce carbon 
footprint. Company has successfully complied with IMO's 0.5% sulphur fuel 
regulation which came into force from January 2020 and all vessels are being 
supplied low sulphur fuel oil since 1st January 2020. This reduction in SOX emitted 
from ships will provide significant health and environmental benefits around the 
world, particularly for coastal populations and those living near ports. It is 
significant to note here that though the company had the option of using 
necessary abatement technology in lieu of using low sulphur fuel such as Exhaust 
Gas cleaning system / scrubber installation to comply with IMO Regulation, 
however the company chose to go for low sulphur fuel oil for all its ships. IMO’s 2023 Greenhouse Gas Emissions strategy has increased the level of 
ambition as follows:
• Carbon intensity of the ship to decline through further improvement of the
 energy efficiency for new ships.
• To reduce CO2 emissions per transport work, as an average across
 international shipping, by at least 40% by 2030.
• Uptake of zero or near-zero GHG emission technologies, fuels and/or energy
 sources to represent at least 5%, striving for 10%, of the energy used by
 international shipping by 2030.
• To peak GHG emissions from international shipping as soon as possible and to
 reach net-zero GHG emissions by or around, i.e., close to, 2050.
(i) Shipbuilding Contract has been signed with an Indian Shipyard for 
construction and delivery of 1 No. 3000 DWT Methanol Dual Fuel Diesel Electric

Green Hydrogen Mission of Govt. of India.

Untreated ballast water poses serious ecological risks as ships become a source 
for transfer of organisms between one ocean to another. A variety of technologies 
are used for ballast water treatment. , these include i.e.: Filtration (physical); 
Chemical Disinfection (oxidizing and non-oxidizing biocides); Ultra-violet 
treatment; De-oxygenation treatment; Heat (thermal treatment) or Magnetic 
Field Treatment. A typical ballast water treatment system on board ships, use two 
or more technologies to ensure that the treated ballast water is compliant with 
the IMO standards.As of 31st March 2026, installation of ballast water treatment 
plant has been completed on all required existing vessels.Shipping Ballast 
Water
The regulations in Annex IV of MARPOL prohibit the discharge of sewage into the 
sea within a specified distance from the nearest land, unless otherwise provided. 
All the Company vessels are fitted with approved Sewage Treatment Plant in 
compliance with IMO’s MAPROL Annex IV requirements.Shipping Domestic 
Sewage 
Discharges
SCI has a zero tolerance policy for Oil Pollution from Ships. Discharge of Oil or oily 
mixture to sea is prohibited from Ships as per Annex – 1 of MARPOL. The vessels are 
constructed in compliance with MARPOL. All vessels are provided with approved 
Oil filtering equipment and all tankers are provided with approved Oil Discharge 
Monitoring and control system. The cargo tanks and pump rooms in tankers are 
provided with double hull to mitigate the risk of oil pollution.Shipping Oil Pollution

the Company's Quality and Environmental Management Systems. The framework is designed to identify 
workplace hazards, assess risks, implement preventive and corrective measures and promote continual 
improvement in occupational health and safety performance.

However, for critical spare parts and proprietary equipment, SCI's Purchase Manual allows procurement from 
the respective Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) or their authorized representatives to ensure 
compatibility, reliability, safety, and compliance with statutory and class requirements. As a result, certain 
equipment and spare parts are necessarily sourced from overseas manufacturers where no equivalent 
Indian alternative is available or where OEM-specific components are required.
Accordingly, while SCI consistently endeavors to maximize procurement from Indian manufacturers and 
suppliers, the nature of international shipping operations and the need to maintain vessel safety, operational 
reliability, and regulatory compliance necessitate the procurement of select equipment and spare parts from 
foreign OEMs.SCI is committed to promoting indigenous manufacturing and, wherever there is sufficient local capacity and 
competition, gives preference to products, equipment, and materials manufactured in India. Procurement of 
general equipment and materials is primarily undertaken through the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) and 
competitive tendering processes, ensuring transparency, and maximum participation of Indian suppliers.
(*) For supply of goods & services in India, procurement is done only from Indian Suppliers, Spare parts from

3.2 Relationship between DirectorsSCI is a Government Company within the meaning of Section 2(45) of the Companies Act, 2013 and the President of India 
presently holds 63.75% of the total paid-up share capital. Accordingly, the power to appoint/remove /nominate Directors 
on the Board of the Company vests with the President of India. As evident from the above table, the composition of Board 
of Directors is not compliant with the requirements of Regulation 17(1) of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015. The Company is 
coordinating with the Competent Authority for filling up the vacant position(s).To this extent, the Company is also non-
compliant with the relevant provisions of DPE Guidelines and the Act. The matter for appointment of requisite number of 
Independent Directors is under active consideration of the Competent Authority.

power to appoint Directors on the Board of SCI vests with the Government of India. The Functional Directors having 
specified skills/ expertise and competencies in the context of Company's business to function efficiently and effectively 
are selected by Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB) whereas Independent Directors are selected from a mix of 
eminent personalities having requisite experience in the diversified fields. The Board comprises of Directors from diverse 
fields, experience, skills, qualifications and competence which are aligned with Company's business, overall strategy, 
values, corporate ethics and culture.

SHARE TRANSFER SYSTEM
Effective from April 01, 2019, SEBI has barred physical transfer of shares of listed companies and mandated transfers 
only through demat. In terms of the SEBI Listing Regulations, securities of the Company can only be transferred in 
dematerialized form. Further, SEBI vide its Circular No. SEBI/HO/MIRSD_RTAMB/P/CIR/2022/8 dated January 24, 2022, 
mandated all the listed companies to issue securities in dematerialized form only, while processing the service request 
for issue of duplicate securities certificates, renewal/exchange of securities certificate, claim from Unclaimed 
Suspense Account, endorsement, sub-division / splitting of securities certificate, consolidation of securities 
certificates/folios, transmission and transposition.
In order to facilitate ease of investing for investors and to secure the rights of investors in the securities which were 
purchased by them, SEBI vide its circular no. SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/97 dated July 02, 2025, notified that 
it has been decided to open a special window only for re-lodgement of transfer deeds, which were lodged prior to the 
deadline of April 01, 2019 and rejected/returned/not attended to due to deficiency in the documents/process/or 
otherwise, for a period of six months from July 07, 2025 till January 06, 2026. Subsequently,  vide its circular no. 
thHO/38/13/11(2)2026-MIRSD-POD/I/3750/2026 dated January 30, 2026, SEBI re-opened the special window for further 
th thperiod of one year from February 05, 2026 to February 04, 2027.
Please note that securities re-lodged for transfers (including those requests that are pending with the listed company / 
RTA, as on date) shall be issued only in demat form following due process. Considering the above, shareholders may 
opt to re-lodge their transfer requests.
In view of the same and to eliminate all risks associated with holding shares in physical form and avail various benefits 
of dematerialization, Members are advised to dematerialize the shares held by them in physical form. Members can 
contact the Company or the Company's Registrar and Share Transfer Agent ('RTA') at  for assistance rta@alankit.com
in this regard. 
In addition, in compliance with regulation 76 of SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 2018, a Reconciliation 
of Share Capital Audit report issued by Practising Company Secretary, confirming that the total issued capital of the 
Company is in agreement with the total number of shares in physical form and the total number of dematerialized 
shares held with National Securities Depository Limited (NSDL) and Central Depository Services (India) Limited (CDSL), is 
submitted to Stock Exchanges and also placed before the Board on a quarterly basis.
SCI's equity shares are compulsorily traded in electronic form. The Company's shares are available for trading in the 
stdepository systems of both NSDL and CDSL. As on 31 March 2026, 99.91% of the paid-up equity share capital, 
representing 46,53,38,223 shares were held in dematerialized form. The processing activities with respect to the 
requests received for dematerialization are completed within 21 days from the date of receipt of request.DEMATERIALIZATION OF SHARES AND LIQUIDITY

22. OUTSTANDING GLOBAL DEPOSITORY RECEIPTS (GDR) OR AMERICAN DEPOSITORY RECEIPTS (ADR) OR WARRANTS OR ANY

In the course of our business activities, financial risks may arise from changes in interest rates and exchange rates. SCI has 
a natural hedge as majority of our receipts are either in foreign currency or are denominated in foreign currency and

unpublished price sensitive information.

44. PROCEEDS FROM PUBLIC ISSUES, RIGHT ISSUES, AND PREFERENTIAL ISSUES ETC
During the year 2010-11, your Company had floated a “Further Public Offer”, (FPO), comprising of a 'fresh issue' of 42,345,365 
equity shares in your company and an 'offer for sale' of 42,345,365 equity shares by the President of India. The FPO 
proceeds of `582.45 crore were fully utilized in the financial year 2011-12 as per object of the issue for part financing of 
capital expenditure on nine shipbuilding projects. However, due to delays in the projects resulting in default by the 
shipyards, during the period January 2014 to May 2014, your Company rescinded contracts for four shipbuilding projects 
and also, re-negotiated the payments for two projects. The investment in the rescinded contracts out of the FPO Proceeds 
was `330.65 crore. Your Company has received back entire sum of `330.65 crore from the shipyards. The shareholders 
vide the resolution passed through postal ballot on 11.02.2017 approved the proposal to re-deploy the said sum of `330.65 
crore received as refund from Shipyards, towards various shipbuilding projects including offshore assets and liquid 
petroleum gas (LPG) vessels and also for acquisition of the any other such vessels, on such terms and conditions as the 
Board would deem fit from time to time as mentioned in the approval of the postal ballot. Further based on the approval 
granted by the shareholders, the Company can also utilize the sum towards the balance payments remaining due for the 
tonnage acquisition made by it. Out of the said amount of `330.65 crore, entire amount has been utilised till date (as on 
31.03.2026) as follows –

267th76 Annual Report 2025-2026  The Members of
1. The Corporate Governance Report prepared by Shipping Corporation of India Limited (hereinafter ‘the 
Company’), contains the details as speciﬁed in regulations 17 to 27, clauses (b) to (i) and (t) of sub-regulation 
2 of regulation 46 and para C, D and E of Schedule V of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing 
Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 as amended (the listing regulations/ SEBI LODR) 
(‘applicable criteria’) for the year ended 31st March, 2026 as required by the Company for annual 
submission to the stock exchange.
Management’s Responsibility
3. The management alongwith the Board of Directors are also responsible for ensuring that the Company 
complies with the conditions of corporate governance as stipulated in the listing regulations, issued by the 
Securities and Exchange Board of India.
Auditor’s Responsibility2. The preparation of the Corporate Governance Report is the responsibility of the management of the 
Company including the preparation and maintenance of all relevant supporting records and documents.  
This responsibility also includes the design, implementation and maintenance of internal control relevant 
to the preparation and presentation of the Corporate Governance Report. 
4. Pursuant to the requirements of the listing regulations, our responsibility is to provide a reasonable 
assurance in the form of an opinion whether, the Company has complied with the conditions of Corporate 
Governance as speciﬁed in the listing regulations.
6. The procedures selected depend on the Auditor’s judgement, including the assessment of the risks 
associated in compliance of the Corporate Governance Guidelines with the applicable criteria.  Summary 
of procedures performed include:
 i) Read and understood the information prepared by the Company and included in its Corporate 
Governance Report.CIN: L63030MH1950GOI008033Shipping Corporation of India Limited 
5. We conducted our examination of the Corporate Governance Report and other relevant records in 
accordance with the Guidance Notes on Certiﬁcation of Corporate Governance issued by the Institute of 
Company Secretaries of India (‘ICSI’).  
 ii) Obtained and veriﬁed that the composition of the Board of Directors with respect to executive and non-
executive directors has been met throughout the reporting period. 
 iii) Obtained and read the Register of Directors as on 31st March, 2026 and veriﬁed that atleast one 
Independent Woman Director was on the Board of Directors throughout the year. UPENDRA SHUKLA & ASSOCIATES

COMMENTS OF THE COMPTROLLER AND AUDITOR GENERAL OF INDIA 
UNDER SECTION 143(6)(b) OF THE COMPANIES ACT, 2013 ON THE 
FINANCIAL STATEMENTS OF THE SHIPPING CORPORATION OF INDIA 
LIMITED,  FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 MARCH 2026
The preparation of financial statements of The Shipping Corporation of India Limited for the year ended 31 
March 2026 in accordance with the financial reporting framework prescribed under the Companies Act, 2013 
(Act) is the responsibility of the management of the company. The statutory auditors appointed by the 
Comptroller and Auditor General of India under section 139 (5) of the Act are responsible for expressing opinion 
on the financial statements under section 143 of the Act based on independent audit in accordance with the 
standards on auditing prescribed under section 143(10) of the Act. This is stated to have been done by them 
vide their Audit Report dated 08.05.2026.
Based on my supplementary audit, I would like to highlight the following significant matters under section 
143(6)(b) of the Act which have come to my attention and which in my view are necessary for enabling a better 
understanding of the financial statements and the related audit report.I, on behalf of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, have conducted a supplementary audit of the 
financial statements of The Shipping Corporation of India Limited for the year ended 31 March 2026 under 
section 143(6)(a) of the Act. This supplementary audit has been carried out independently without access to 
the working papers of the statutory auditors and is limited primarily to inquiries of the statutory auditors and 
company personnel and a selective examination of some of the accounting records.
Comments on Disclosures
Comment No. 1
Notes to Standalone Financial Statements for the financial year 2025-26
The Company accounted  ₹10.85 crore as grant received during 2025-26, for operation of cargo shipping 
services between India and Maldives which was adjusted against operating expenditure. However, the 
Significant Accounting Policy of the Company was deficient to the extent of non- disclosure of (a) its 
accounting policy on Government grants (including method of presentation in financial statements) and (b) 
comment on unfulfilled conditions and other contingencies attached to Government assistance that has 
been recognized as mandated by Ind AS 20 (Para 39).
Comment No. 2
Notes to Standalone Financial Statements for the financial year 2025-26
The Company received Income Tax refund order and refund amount during March and April 2026. However, 
the Company did not recognize the refund on accrual basis in the financial statements. However, the 
deviation from accrual basis of accounting as per Ind AS 1 (Para 27) for the income tax refunds and interest 
receivable on same was not disclosed in the notes to the financial statements as mandated by Ind AS 1. Thus, 
accounting of  income tax refunds and interest received was in deviation to Ind AS 1 requirements.

Opinion
We have audited the accompanying Standalone Financial Statements of The Shipping Corporation of India 
Limited (“the Company”), which comprise the Balance Sheet as at 31.03.2026, the Statement of Proﬁt and Loss 
(including Other Comprehensive Income), the Statement of Changes in Equity and the Statement of Cash Flows 
for the year then ended, and notes to the Standalone Financial Statements including a summary of signiﬁcant 
accounting policies and other explanatory information (hereinafter referred to as “Standalone Financial 
Statements”).
In our opinion and to the best of our information and according to the explanations given to us, the aforesaid 
Standalone Financial Statements give the information required by the Companies Act, 2013 (“the Act”) in the 
manner so required and give a true and fair view in conformity with the Indian Accounting Standards  prescribed 
under section 133 of the Act read with the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015, as amended, 
(“Ind AS”), and other accounting principles generally accepted in India, of the state of affairs of the Company as at 
31.03.2026, its proﬁt (including other comprehensive income), changes in equity and its cash ﬂows for the year 
ended on that date.
Basis for Opinion
We conducted our audit of the Standalone Financial Statements in accordance with Standards on Auditing (SAs) 
speciﬁed under section 143(10) of the Act. Our responsibilities under those Standards are further described in the 
Auditor's Responsibilities for the Audit of the Standalone Financial Statements section of our report. We are 
independent of the Company in accordance with the Code of Ethics issued by the Institute of Chartered 
Accountants of India (“ICAI”) together with the ethical requirements that are relevant to our audit of the 
Standalone Financial Statements under the provisions of the Act and Rules made thereunder, and we have 
fulﬁlled our other ethical responsibilities in accordance with these requirements and the ICAI's Code of Ethics. We 
believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufﬁcient and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion 
on the Standalone Financial Statements.
Key Audit Matters 
Key audit matters are those matters that, in our professional judgment, were of most signiﬁcance in our audit of 
the Standalone Financial Statements of the current year. These matters were addressed in the context of our 
audit of the Standalone Financial Statements as a whole, and in forming our opinion thereon, and we do not 
provide a separate opinion on these matters. We have determined the matters described below to be the key 
audit matters to be communicated in our report.

Responsibilities of Management and Those Charged with Governance for the Standalone Financial

Act with respect to the preparation of these Standalone Financial Statements that give a true and fair view of the 
ﬁnancial position, ﬁnancial performance (including other comprehensive income), changes in equity and cash 
ﬂows of the Company in accordance with the Ind AS and other accounting principles generally accepted in India. 
This responsibility also includes maintenance of adequate accounting records in accordance with the provisions 
of the Act for safeguarding of the assets of the Company and for preventing and detecting frauds and other 
irregularities; selection and application of appropriate accounting policies; making judgments and estimates 
that are reasonable and prudent; and design, implementation and maintenance of adequate internal ﬁnancial 
controls, that were operating effectively for ensuring the accuracy and completeness of the accounting records, 
relevant to the preparation and presentation of the Standalone Financial Statements that give a true and fair view 
and are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error.When we read the other information, If we conclude that there is a material misstatement therein, we are required 
to communicate the matters to those charged with governance and determine the actions under the applicable 
laws and regulations. 
Our objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the Standalone Financial Statements as a 
whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and to issue an auditor's report that 
includes our opinion. Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance, but is not a guarantee that an audit 
conducted in accordance with SAs will always detect a material misstatement when it exists. Misstatements can 
arise from fraud or error and are considered material if, individually or in the aggregate, they could reasonably be 
expected to inﬂuence the economic decisions of users taken on the basis of this Standalone Financial Statements.  In connection with our audit of the Standalone Financial Statements, our responsibility is to read the other 
information and, in doing so, consider whether the other information is materially inconsistent with the 
Standalone Financial Statements or our knowledge obtained in the audit or otherwise appears to be materially 
misstated.

We have audited the internal ﬁnancial controls with reference to Standalone Financial Statements of The 
Shipping Corporation of India Limited (“the Company”) as of 31.03.2026 in conjunction with our audit of the 
Standalone Financial Statements of the Company for the year ended on that date.
Management’s Responsibility for Internal Financial ControlsReport on the Internal Financial Controls with reference to Standalone Financial Statements under clause (i) of 
sub-section 3 of section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013 (“the Act”)
The Company’s management is responsible for establishing and maintaining internal ﬁnancial controls based on 
the internal control with reference to ﬁnancial statements criteria established by the Company considering the 
essential components of internal control stated in the Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls Over 
Financial Reporting (the “Guidance Note”) issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (“ICAI”). These 
responsibilities include the design, implementation and maintenance of adequate internal ﬁnancial controls that 
were operating effectively for ensuring the orderly and efﬁcient conduct of its business, including adherence to 
Company’s policies, the safeguarding of its assets, the prevention and detection of frauds and errors, the 
accuracy and completeness of the accounting records, and the timely preparation of reliable ﬁnancial 
information, as required under the Act.
Auditors’ Responsibility
Our audit of internal ﬁnancial controls with reference to ﬁnancial statements included obtaining an 
understanding of internal ﬁnancial controls with reference to ﬁnancial statements, assessing the risk that a 
material weakness exists, and testing and evaluating the design and operating effectiveness of internal controls 
based on the assessed risk. The procedures selected depend on the auditor’s judgment, including the 
assessment of the risks of material misstatement of the ﬁnancial statements, whether due to fraud or error.
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufﬁcient and appropriate to provide a basis for our audit 
opinion on the Company’s internal ﬁnancial controls with reference to ﬁnancial statements.Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the Company's internal ﬁnancial controls with reference to ﬁnancial 
statements based on our audit. We conducted our audit in accordance with the Guidance Note and the 
Standards on Auditing speciﬁed under section 143(10) of the Act to the extent applicable to an audit of internal 
ﬁnancial controls, both issued by the ICAI. Those Standards and the Guidance Note require that we comply with 
ethical requirements and plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether adequate 
internal ﬁnancial controls with reference to ﬁnancial statements was established and maintained and if such 
controls operated effectively in all material respects.
Our audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit evidence about the adequacy of the internal ﬁnancial 
controls with reference to ﬁnancial statements and their operating effectiveness.
Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with reference to Financial Statements
A company's internal ﬁnancial control with reference to ﬁnancial statements is a process designed to provide 
reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of ﬁnancial reporting and the preparation of ﬁnancial statements 
288 The Shipping Corpor ation of India LimitedANNEXURE TO THE INDEPENDENT AUDITOR’S REPORT
=== page 292 ===
In our opinion, and to the best of our information and according to explanations given to us, the Company has, in 
all material respects, adequate internal ﬁnancial controls with reference to ﬁnancial statements and such 
internal ﬁnancial controls with reference to ﬁnancial statements were operating effectively as at 31.03.2026,

the possibility of collusion or improper management override of controls, material misstatements due to error or 
fraud may occur and not be detected. Also, projections of any evaluation of the internal ﬁnancial controls with 
reference to ﬁnancial statements to future periods are subject to the risk that the internal ﬁnancial controls with 
reference to ﬁnancial statements may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree 
of compliance with the policies or procedures may deteriorate.

No Impact To determine Impairment of each vessel, carrying 
amount of the vessel is compared with its recoverable 
amount. Where the carrying amount of the vessel 
exceeds the recoverable amount, an impairment 
loss for the vessel is recognized. Recoverable 
amount of the vessel is higher of its Market Value or 
Value in use as on the balance sheet date. Market 
value of vessels at Balance Sheet date are based on 
valuation reports provided by reputed valuation 
ﬁrms. Value in use of vessels is based on projections 
of Future Cash inﬂows & Outﬂows generated from 
the use of the vessel and its subsequent sale. Cash 
inﬂows and outﬂows used in the calculation are 
based on market report of research and advisory 
ﬁrms as well as best available management 
estimates. Cash Inﬂow on sale of vessels is considered 
as their Scrap Value at the end of their useful life. The 
Value in use of Vessels as on the reporting date is 
arrived at by discounting the Net Cash Inﬂows by 
using Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC).State the system for providing 
Impairment to vessels.1As per DPE Guidelines where a listed Central Public

the company's board does not meet the mandatory

the latest amendments issued by DPE, however

1.2 Foreign Currency Translation
 (a) Functional and Presentational Currency
  Items included in the Standalone Financial Statements of the Company are measured using the 
currency of the primary economic environment in which the entity operates (‘the functional currency’). 
The Standalone Financial Statements are presented in ‘Indian Rupees’ (INR), which is the Company’s 
functional and presentation currency.
 (b) Transactions and Balances
1.3 Property, Plant and Equipment  Non-monetary items carried at fair value that are denominated in foreign currencies are retranslated at 
the rates prevailing at the date when the fair value is determined. Non-monetary items that are 
measured in terms of historical cost in a foreign currency are not retranslated.  b) In respect of long term loans taken after 31.03.2016, the exchange difference is charged / credited to 
Statement of Proﬁt & Loss.  a) In respect of long term loans outstanding as on 31.03.2016, exchange difference is adjusted in the 
carrying cost of respective assets. 
  The exchange differences arising on translation of other monetary assets and liabilities are recognised 
in the Statement of proﬁt and loss.
 Items of property, plant and equipment acquired or constructed are stated at historical cost net of 
recoverable taxes, less accumulated depreciation and accumulated impairment of loss, if any. The cost of 
tangible assets comprises of its purchase price, borrowing costs and adjustment arising for exchange rate 
variations attributable to the assets, wherever applicable including any cost directly attributable till 
completion of maiden voyage for bringing the asset to the condition of its intended use. In respect of second-  Exchange difference arising on repayment of liabilities and conversion of foreign currency closing 
balances pertaining to long term loans for acquiring ships / containers / other depreciable assets and 
asset under construction is recognised as follows:  The foreign currency balances in US Dollars, UK Pounds, Euro and Japanese YEN appearing in the books of 
account at the period end are translated into Indian Rupees at the available RBI reference 
rate/exchange rate published through FBIL at the period end. The foreign currency balances other than 
US Dollars, UK Pounds, Euro and Japanese YEN appearing in the books of account at the period end are 
translated into Indian Rupees at the rate available on xe.com website at the period end. Thereafter, the 
monetary assets and monetary liabilities as well as the Long Term Loans are translated into rupees at 
rate prevailing at the period end.  All foreign currency transactions are recorded at the previous day’s available RBI reference 
rate/exchange rate published through FBIL (Financial Benchmarks India Private Limited). Since the RBI 
reference rate published through FBIL is available for four major currencies only i.e. USD, GBP, EUR, YEN, 
exchange rates of other currencies are taken from xe.com website.
